chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: Warsh gave no hint at 10:30pm CT — 'I don't prejudge meetings' — so October stays ~30% into Saturday's blackout; the 10-year fell to ~5.04% in Asia and DXY closed at 102.05 (-0.48%).
chapters.meaning: What changed: Fed Chair Warsh, in the Bangkok fireside with Georgieva, said he does not 'prejudge' rate decisions — 'It's a new chapter at the Fed, we're not in that business anymore' — and offered no signal on October 27-28. Those were his last public words before Saturday's blackout. The pricing barely moved: ~70.7% hold / ~30% hike for October. December is the loose end — one desk read put it at ~67% while LSEG had ~90%+ Thursday, and that split is flagged, not settled. The hawkish chorus hardened around him: Hammack warned that slipping inflation expectations would require the Fed to move 'even more' ('hearing more from lower income Americans struggling with inflation'), and Goolsbee called it 'a discouraging month in terms of inflation.' The 10-year closed at 5.10% (-9bp) and slipped to ~5.04% in Asia — the softest in about a month — and DXY closed 102.047 (-0.48%), retreating from Wednesday's 18-month high. Thread: Thursday's edition said the market ignored the hot PPI (+1.3%, biggest since March 2022), October faded to ~29%, and the October question was about the calendar (midterms), not the data — with Warsh as the last voice before the blackout. What it means: confirms. Warsh didn't re-arm the hike (Thursday's bull scenario did not play out); the 'no prejudge' line locks in the priced hold, and the December split is now the live pricing question. The four-beat read on the number: (1) October pricing sits near ~30% for a hike — the market's bet on what the Fed does in twelve days; (2) it barely moved on Warsh's non-signal, because a non-signal from the chair into blackout IS the signal — no rescue for the hike camp; (3) ~30% with the 10-year at one-month lows means the bond market has stopped believing the October hike story even as Fed speakers keep talking hawkish; (4) for the dollar, the question that matters into the blackout is no longer 'will they' but 'what breaks the hold pricing' — and only Friday's data or a weekend shock can do it now.
chapters.fx: What to watch: import prices 7:30am CT (consensus +0.8% m/m) and industrial production 8:15am CT (consensus +0.4%) — the last hard data before the blackout; September budget balance 1pm CT (consensus -$34.7B) and TIC flows 3pm CT. Correction: US housing starts are NOT today — September starts print Tuesday Oct 20. Blackout from Saturday; September PCE lands Oct 29, the day after the meeting.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: EUR/USD closed +0.56% at ~1.1218 — the biggest daily gain in ~2 months — on the dollar fade, not euro strength; the 4am CT final CPI confirms or revises the 3.8% flash.
chapters.meaning: What changed: EUR/USD closed Thursday at ~1.1218 (+0.56%), its biggest daily gain in about two months, and held ~1.1232 in Asia — fully recovered from the post-CPI low near 1.1114. The euro's own news was the calendar, not a surprise: the final September CPI prints at 4am CT, confirming or revising the flash — 3.8% headline (which beat the 3.6% consensus) and 2.5% core. That flash beat is new context for the site: the ECB's December-hike case has hotter cover than the French number alone suggested. Thread: Thursday's edition said the pair trades the Fed leg, not the ECB leg, with Simkus ('additional evidence suggesting some tightening may be necessary') as the steadier leg. What it means: confirms — the pair is still a dollar story; the euro leg's job is to not get in the way, and a 3.8% confirm does exactly that. The four-beat read: (1) 3.8% is the share of the eurozone price basket that got more expensive over a year — nearly double the ECB's 2% target; (2) it beat the 3.6% consensus, so the surprise leans hawkish; (3) ~3.8% annualized pressure vs 2% target is why December, not October 29 (~12%), is the ECB's live meeting; (4) for the euro, hotter inflation with a hiking ECB underneath is the floor — the ceiling is still the dollar leg and the French fiscal drag.
chapters.fx: What to watch: final CPI 4am CT (confirm-or-revise 3.8% / core 2.5%); Nagel speaks Saturday; France's revenue-section vote Oct 20 and Moody's Oct 23.

chapters.teaser: Bailey spoke overnight (~2am CT): second-round pressures 'quite subdued' so far, but August's 3.1% CPI 'enormously frustrating' — cable rose to ~1.326-1.331 on the dollar fade.
chapters.meaning: What changed: Bailey's IIF appearance (verified overnight, ~2am CT) gave the market two lines: second-round inflation pressures look 'so far... quite subdued,' while August's 3.1% CPI was 'enormously frustrating' — the Middle East blamed — and it's 'too early to conclude.' Cable closed ~1.3259 (+0.5%+) and touched ~1.3310 in Asia, riding the dollar fade. Correction: UK retail sales are NOT today — the ONS September release is due ~Oct 23; only survey reads (BRC/Barclays) are out. Thread: Thursday's edition said 54 of 63 economists expect the November hike to 4.00%, with Pill capping the 2027 path ('need not be the start of a long series'). What it means: confirms — Bailey didn't touch November (~86%+ priced); his 'subdued' second-round read is dovish-leaning texture for the 2027 path, sitting with Pill against the market's four-hikes-by-September-2027 pricing. The four-beat read: (1) 3.1% is August CPI — more than 50% above the BoE's 2% target, and 'frustrating' because energy, not demand, is doing it; (2) no surprise vs the priced November hike — the news is what he said about AFTER; (3) 'subdued' second-round effects mean the 3.1% isn't yet embedding into wages — the thing the BoE actually hikes against; (4) for sterling, the November hike is the floor and the 2027 path is the trade — Bailey just leaned the path dovish.

chapters.teaser: USD/JPY faded to 157.92 (-0.34%) with the 10-year, and a US Treasury undersecretary said in Bangkok that 'yen level and monetary policy must change' — rhetorical pressure on top of Koeda's hawkishness.
chapters.meaning: What changed: USD/JPY closed at 157.92 (-0.34%), range 157.58-158.33, and sat ~157.8-158.18 in Asia — still breathing with the US yield leg as the 10-year fell to one-month lows. The new voice is American: Treasury Undersecretary Browne said in Bangkok that 'Japan no longer faces a deflationary environment; yen level and monetary policy must change' — a US official commenting on the yen's level, which is its own kind of intervention risk. Thread: Thursday's edition said Koeda keeps December alive (>80%, October ~9-10%), the haven bid picked the franc first, and 160 is the intervention line. What it means: confirms the December-not-October shape — Browne's line adds US-side rhetorical pressure for the BoJ to move, which is yen-supportive at the margin but changes no pricing tonight. The four-beat read: (1) 157.92 is how many yen a dollar buys — the pair fell as US yields fell; (2) no surprise in the move, it tracked the 10-year; (3) the pair lives on the US-Japan rate gap, and a falling 10-year narrows it; (4) for the yen, the question is still December — Browne just made the US a louder voice in that room.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The positioning lens switches to the hedge-fund cut — and it breaks the squeeze story: funds are net LONG AUD at the 79th percentile, not at record shorts; the real-money book is short at the 17th, leaning the other way.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the methodology, and it matters. The positioning feed now reads the CFTC Traders in Financial Futures cut (hedge funds & CTAs, the file Claude's action builds) — and on that cut, hedge funds are net long the aussie at the 79th percentile of their own history, having added 4,354 contracts over four weeks. The 'record shorts, squeeze-loaded' read came from the legacy non-commercial series; the TFF cut disagrees. The genuine tension is the split: real money is net short at the 17th percentile — the two books lean opposite ways. AUD/USD closed ~0.6928 (-0.59%), Asia 0.6916-0.6948, still the soft leg on the jobs miss (-39.3K, unemployment 4.7%, a five-year high). Thread: Thursday's edition said the jobs miss collided with the risk-off tape, November-hike odds pared, and the record-shorts squeeze needed the RBA to look through the miss. What it means: breaks part of the thesis — the squeeze pillar of the bull case rested on the legacy cut; on the TFF cut the fast-money book is already long, so a dovish surprise has more room to hurt than a hawkish one has to help. The four-beat read: (1) 79th percentile means hedge funds are longer AUD than in roughly four-fifths of their history since 2015; (2) that's the opposite of the 'record short' story — the surprise is the disagreement between the two CFTC cuts; (3) long books are vulnerable to dovish news (unwind risk), which is exactly what the jobs miss delivered; (4) for the aussie, the positioning edge now sits with real money's short — a hawkish RBA surprise would squeeze them, not the hedge funds.
chapters.fx: What to watch: RBA's Kent speaks Saturday; China Q3 GDP Monday (consensus 4.4% y/y); RBA Nov 2-3 is the verdict on whether the tightening bias survives the jobs miss.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: Two-way data for the two-way bet: BNZ PMI 56.5 — the strongest since 2021 — feeds the hike side, but flat food prices and a second month of falling card spending feed the hold side.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the overnight prints split neatly. The BNZ-BusinessNZ PMI hit 56.5 in September (August revised to 53.3) — the strongest since 2021 outside one spike, the 15th straight month of expansion, employment back in expansion at 51.8. Against it: food prices were flat m/m (0.0% vs +0.3% in August; 2.4% y/y) and card retail spending fell 0.4% — the second straight monthly fall. NZD/USD closed ~0.5635 and traded 0.5614-0.5658 in Asia, still hovering above the 52-week low near 0.5580. Thread: Thursday's edition said Conway called Oct 28 'wide open' with the direction 'most likely up,' and NZ CPI Oct 21 settles it. What it means: confirms the two-way bet — the PMI is the hike side's best exhibit, the flat food print plus soft card spending is the hold side's. Neither settles anything; Oct 21 does. The four-beat read: (1) 56.5 is a diffusion index — above 50 means manufacturing is expanding, and 56.5 is brisk; (2) it beat August's 53.3, so the surprise is acceleration, not just expansion; (3) factories humming while consumers pull back is the RBNZ's dilemma in miniature — growth vs demand; (4) for the kiwi, the question into Oct 28 is which half the board weights — and flat food prices just lightened the hike side's load.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Escalation and release pulled opposite ways overnight: CENTCOM confirmed an Iranian projectile sank a Hormuz container ship and Houthis hit Aden — while the IEA accelerated a ~100M-bbl release. Spread compressed to ~$8.30.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the two-way pull, itemized. Escalation: US CENTCOM confirmed the container ship that sank in Hormuz this week was struck by an Iranian projectile — the first official US attribution of a direct Iranian military strike on commercial shipping in the strait; the Houthis fired five missiles at Aden's presidential palace, killing two guards; Eurasia Group put escalation odds at 65%; Hormuz clearance averaged 11.62M bpd over the seven days to Oct 13 — about 68% of the 17.15M baseline. Release: the IEA agreed Thursday to accelerate the remaining ~100M barrels of the March collective action (over 330M already released of 400M+ pledged), including 20M+ barrels of diesel 'as soon as possible'; the Trump administration is weighing lifting sanctions on some shadow-fleet tankers to ease record freight rates. Price: Brent settled Thursday at $105.92 (-14¢), WTI +3.03% at $97.97 on the EIA draw; Friday Asia had Brent at $105.51 (-0.67%) and WTI at $97.20 (-0.79%) — the spread compressed to ~$8.31 from ~$9.70. Thread: Thursday's edition said Brent $104-108 holds until a verified shock or ceasefire, and the spread reads the premium as shipping risk, not demand. What it means: confirms the range — the release news leaked the freight premium (the spread's compression is the tell) while the escalation news kept the floor; neither side broke. Correction to Thursday's edition: the 'Saturday-evening Hormuz deadline' framing doesn't check out — no such Trump statement was found; the risk is the escalation itself, not a clock. The four-beat read: (1) ~$8.30 is the Brent-WTI spread — what the world pays over the US price for seaborne crude; (2) it compressed ~$1.40 as the freight premium leaked on shadow-fleet chatter; (3) a wide spread means the market is pricing shipping risk, not demand — the premium lives in the tanker, not the barrel; (4) for FX, the spread is the CAD-vs-JPY/EUR tell — wide favors the exporter, narrow relieves the importers. Positioning footnote: hedge funds sit crowded short WTI (5th percentile, lightest in 12 weeks) — a verified supply shock would squeeze, not just rally.
chapters.fx: What to watch: any new Hormuz incident or US decision on shadow-fleet relief; whether the IEA diesel hits the market; spread toward $15 = Hormuz risk back in force; toward $5 = premium truly unwinding. Friday US data for the demand leg.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: The anti-dollar bid held: spot closed ~$4,158-4,159 (+1.3%) and sat ~$4,172 in Asia as the 10-year fell to one-month lows — silver ran +3.2% to $57.31 alongside.
chapters.meaning: What changed: gold's Thursday rally held — spot closed ~$4,158-4,159 (+1.3%), COMEX $4,177.50, and Asia kept ~$4,172 (+0.1%). Silver ran harder: +3.2% to $57.31, $57.81 in Asia. The driver is the rate leg: the 10-year at ~5.04% in Asia is the softest in about a month, and the dollar faded with it. The fear leg cooled at the margin — Thursday's session was the relief bounce: the Nasdaq 100 fell as much as 3.28% intraday and closed roughly flat (+0.08% Nasdaq Comp; Dow +1.08%, S&P +0.33%) on bargain hunting and falling yields; Asia woke up green (Kospi +3.3%, Nikkei +1.9%, Hang Seng +1.0%). CoreWeave rebounded 6% after Jensen Huang said it needs no financial support (its 2032 bonds still ~15%); BTC fell below $80k then bounced to ~$82,000 in Asia. Thread: Thursday's edition said the rate leg easing re-armed the anti-dollar bid and gold is the haven that works when FX havens hesitate. What it means: confirms — both engines still bid, with the rate leg doing the work and the fear leg idling. The four-beat read: (1) $4,172 is gold's price — up ~1.3% on the day; (2) it rose as the 10-year fell, the classic inverse relationship holding; (3) lower real yields cut the opportunity cost of holding metal — gold pays no yield, so it wins when bonds pay less; (4) for FX, firm gold with a soft dollar is the anti-dollar trade in one line — it says the market is hedging the Fed, not just fearing the headlines.
